drills.title: Reversion on forward NOI
drills.question: Year 5 NOI is $2,000,000 and grows 3% into Year 6. You sell at the end of Year 5 at a 6.50% cap with 2% selling costs. Compute the net reversion, and how much an analyst understates it by capitalizing Year 5 NOI.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing trailing (Year 5) NOI with a cap rate quoted on forward NOI
Forgetting selling costs
drills.intuition: The buyer at exit pays for the income they will receive, which is Year 6 NOI.
drills.takeaway: Terminal value always uses NOI(T+1). A one-year slip is worth about g/c of the reversion: here 3%/6.5% of nothing but timing.

drills.title: Loaded cap rate with reassessment
drills.question: NOI before property tax is $1,500,000. After a sale the assessor sets assessed value at 80% of price; the tax rate is 2.2%. The market cap rate on NOI after tax is 7.0%. Value the property, and state the overstatement if you capitalize pre-tax NOI at 7.0%.
common_mistakes: Applying the tax rate to 100% of price without stating the assessment ratio
Capitalizing the seller's (lower) tax bill
drills.intuition: Tax depends on the price, and the price depends on the tax; the loaded cap solves both at once.
drills.takeaway: In reassessment jurisdictions, underwrite tax on your price, never on the seller's bill.

drills.title: What must the buyer believe at a 4.75% cap?
drills.question: An apartment portfolio trades at a 4.75% cap. Buyers require 7.0% unlevered and long-run capex is 6% of NOI. What perpetual NOI growth does the price imply? Is that plausible, and what would you check?

rubric: Compares with a stated long-run inflation and real rent growth view, labeled as an assumption
Notes that ignoring capex would overstate implied growth's cushion (k - c = 2.25% vs 2.535%)
Names checks: new supply pipeline, rent-to-income ratios, expense growth (insurance, tax)

drills.solution: c(1 - kappa) = 0.0475 x 0.94 = 4.465%. g = 7.00% - 4.465% = 2.535%. The price is a bet that NOI grows near or slightly above long-run inflation forever. Whether that is plausible depends on supply and expense growth; the arithmetic tells you which belief to test.
common_mistakes: Using g = k - c and ignoring capex
Treating the implied growth as a forecast rather than as the belief the price requires
drills.intuition: A cap rate is k minus g, grossed up for capital spending.
drills.takeaway: Reverse-engineer every price into an implied growth or return, then argue about that number.

drills.title: Trailing versus stabilized NOI in a bid
drills.question: A small industrial building is 70% leased. Trailing NOI is $720,000; underwritten stabilized NOI is $900,000 after lease-up, which will cost $650,000 in downtime, TI and commissions. The market cap is 6.25% on stabilized NOI. Compute the as-is value and the trailing-NOI value, and say which you would bid and why.

rubric: Trailing value 11,520,000 is a convention mismatch, not a conservative value
Bid below as-is to price lease-up risk (not just cost); states the size of the risk discount and why
Names evidence that would close the gap (signed LOIs, broker tours, comparable lease-ups)

drills.solution: Stabilized value = 900,000/0.0625 = 14,400,000. As-is = 14,400,000 - 650,000 = 13,750,000. Trailing value = 720,000/0.0625 = 11,520,000. Bid from as-is less a risk discount for the lease-up; the trailing value misapplies a stabilized cap rate to unstabilized income.
common_mistakes: Paying stabilized value for an unstabilized asset
Calling the trailing-NOI value conservative
drills.intuition: Cap rates are quoted on stabilized forward income; adjust the income, not the cap rate.
drills.takeaway: As-is value = stabilized value minus the cost and the risk of getting there.

drills.title: Cap +100 bp, NOI -5%, 65% LTV
drills.question: Cap rates rise from 5.5% to 6.5% and NOI falls 5%. What is the change in asset value, and in equity at 65% LTV (debt unchanged)?
common_mistakes: Adding -5% and -15.4% (the components do not add; they multiply)
Dividing by 0.65 instead of 0.35
drills.intuition: Leverage divides the asset move by the equity share.
drills.takeaway: A 20% asset decline at 65% LTV removes more than half the equity and moves LTV past most refinancing limits.

drills.title: Residual land value and a 50 bp cap move
drills.question: A build-to-rent project has stabilized NOI of $2.4m. Hard $28.0m, soft $5.6m, financing $2.2m, selling costs 1.5%, required margin 15% on total cost. Compute residual land value at a 5.50% and a 6.00% exit cap. The landowner wants $3.0m. Advise the developer.

rubric: Recognizes the $3.0m ask exceeds residual value even at 5.50%
Advises an option or a price tied to entitlement/rates rather than a firm purchase; notes land is a levered call on cap rates

common_mistakes: Applying the margin to value instead of cost
Forgetting selling costs
drills.intuition: Land absorbs every change in GDV after fixed costs and margin.
drills.takeaway: Do not buy land outright at a price that requires today's cap rate to hold; buy an option.

drills.title: The IRR identity and a 50 bp exit-cap stress
drills.question: You buy at a 5.25% going-in cap, NOI grows 2.5% a year, no capex, no transaction costs, 5-year hold. (a) What is the IRR if you exit at 5.25% on Year 6 NOI? (b) What if you exit at 5.75%?

rubric: (a) uses the identity IRR = c + g = 7.75% without a calculator
(b) computes about 6.09%
States that a 50 bp exit move costs about 166 bp of IRR over five years
Labels the difference between (a) and (b) as a cap-rate forecast, not a business plan

drills.solution: (a) With flat cap, constant growth, no capex or costs, IRR = c + g = 5.25% + 2.5% = 7.75% exactly. (b) Price 1/0.0525 = 19.048 per $1 of NOI; reversion = 1.025^5/0.0575 = 19.677; flows give IRR = 6.09%.
common_mistakes: Thinking the identity needs a long hold; it holds for any hold length
Ignoring that the exit cap applies to NOI(T+1)
drills.intuition: If nothing about the pricing changes, you earn the yield plus the growth.
drills.takeaway: Every basis point of IRR above c + g is a claim about exit pricing, capex, or growth beyond trend.

drills.title: Three anchors and a maturity
drills.question: An owner says: 'I have $15.0m in this hotel, it appraised at $17.2m two years ago, and replacement cost is $165k a key ($19.8m). I'll take $16.5m.' T-12 NOI after a 4% reserve is $1.05m; your market cap range is 9.0%-10.5%. The $11.8m loan matures in 10 months. Write the analysis you would give your committee and the approach you would take with the owner.

rubric: Values the hotel on normalized NOI: 1.05m/9.0%-10.5% = $11.7m-$10.0m before any PIP or normalization; states that the T-12 must be normalized (Case A)
Identifies basis as sunk, the appraisal as stale (decomposes the gap into NOI and cap-rate effects if data allow), and replacement cost as a supply ceiling not a floor
Recognizes the loan ($11.8m) is near or above value, so the owner may be unable to sell without bringing cash; computes the payoff price after selling costs
Proposes a strategy keyed to the maturity: an offer with an expiry, a discussion with the lender, or patience; names what would raise or lower the bid
States that no transaction may be possible before maturity and that abstention with a re-engagement trigger is acceptable

drills.solution: Value is about $10.0-11.7m on the stated NOI, 29-39% below the ask. None of the three anchors is value evidence. The owner's constraint is the loan: at ~$12.0-12.2m gross (after 2-3% selling costs) the owner merely repays the debt. A sale near value requires the owner to bring cash, so expect an extension request first. The professional approach is to put a price with conditions and an expiry in front of the owner, share the arithmetic the lender will apply, and be ready at maturity.
common_mistakes: Treating replacement cost as a floor
Splitting the difference between the ask and value
Ignoring the loan's effect on the owner's ability to sell
drills.intuition: Anchors predict the seller's behavior; constraints predict when that behavior changes.
drills.takeaway: Bid on cash flow; time the bid to the constraint that releases the anchor.

drills.title: Break-even exit cap that straddles your range
drills.question: You can buy at $20.0m (6.50% going-in on Year 1 NOI of $1.3m), NOI growth 2%, 5-year hold, no capex or costs. Your target is 8.0% unlevered. Find the exit cap at which IRR = 8.0%. Your honest exit-cap range is 6.0%-7.0%. Bid, pass, or gather information?

rubric: Solves the break-even exit cap of about 6.68%
Recognizes the 6.0%-7.0% range straddles the break-even, so the decision depends on an unknown
Recommends gathering information (recent trades, debt-market depth, supply) or lowering price until the break-even sits above 7.0%; abstention is the right answer if neither is possible
Computes or estimates the price at which a 7.0% exit still yields 8%

drills.solution: IRR is 9.95% at a 6.0% exit and 7.18% at 7.0%; it crosses 8.0% at an exit cap of 6.68%. Your range straddles that value, so at $20.0m the decision rests on a cap-rate forecast you cannot defend. Pass at this price, or bid lower so that a 7.0% exit still clears 8%.
common_mistakes: Using the midpoint of the range (6.5%) as if it were known and bidding confidently
Assuming exit cap = going-in cap
drills.intuition: Break-even analysis tells you whether your ignorance matters.
drills.takeaway: When your range straddles break-even, abstain or change the price; do not guess.

drills.title: Negative leverage: equity IRR below property IRR
drills.question: A $10.0m asset with flat NOI of $650,000 (6.50% cap) is financed with a 60% interest-only loan at 7.0%. Five-year hold, no costs. Compute the equity IRR if you exit at 6.50% and at 7.00%. Explain the first answer without a calculator.
common_mistakes: Assuming leverage always raises return
Ignoring the exit-cap effect, which leverage magnifies
drills.intuition: Borrowing at 7% to own a 6.5% asset lowers the return unless the asset appreciates.
drills.takeaway: With negative leverage, every unit of debt is a bet on appreciation.
